title: status and snapshot read unbounded direct-child files before any cap
attack_steps: A lower-trust content contributor places a very large or sparse regular direct-child file in a scope the victim uses.
The victim runs status or snapshot on that scope.
The working-tree builder accepts the file through the type, name, and exclusion filters and calls fs::read before applying any byte ceiling.
The victim process allocates and reads attacker-sized bytes; snapshot can additionally copy them into the archive, causing command failure or substantial local resource pressure.
assumptions: The selected scope is shared, supplied, or otherwise writable by a lower-trust content contributor.
The hostile file is a direct regular child and is not explicitly excluded.
The victim invokes a routine status or snapshot command.
context: KCS has no listener; this is a filesystem-mediated availability path. Impact crosses from lower-trust scope content into the victim KCS process, but remains local, recoverable, and limited to the selected workflow.
in_scope: yes; untrusted direct-child files and bounded local processing are explicit threat-model surfaces under I6 and I12
exposure: not public; reachable through local CLI processing of an adopted or shared scope
identity: KCS runs as the victim OS user with that user's filesystem and memory limits; the attacker needs no KCS or OS-administrator identity
cross_boundary: yes; lower-trust file size crosses the scope-content boundary into victim-process memory, I/O, and archive storage
preconditions: plausible: control one included direct-child file and wait for the operator to run status or snapshot; sparse files can make the logical-size amplification inexpensive
attacker_control: yes; the lower-trust contributor controls the included file's logical size and bytes
category: resource consumption / local denial of service (CWE-400, CWE-770)
mitigations: Subdirectories, symlinks observed at enumeration, non-regular entries, and explicit exclusions are skipped.
Status does not persist the bytes and snapshot holds the store lock.
The operator can remove the hostile file and retry.
auth_scope: internal-only; local filesystem and CLI surface with no network authentication boundary
impact_surface: runtime memory and I/O; snapshot also affects archive disk usage
target_reach: one KCS process and selected scope per invocation
counterevidence: The later effective_max_input_bytes control applies only to adapter processing and does not protect status or snapshot.
The command is recoverable after removing the file and does not create a confidentiality or authorization bypass.
blindspots: No large or sparse-file runtime measurement was retained; actual failure thresholds depend on host limits.
rationale: A realistic lower-trust scope contributor can deterministically reach a victim resource sink through routine commands, so self-only suppression does not apply. The required matrix maps medium impact plus high likelihood to medium.

title: Mistral OCR responses lack read, body, cardinality, and persistence bounds

affected_locations.label: OCR POST and full JSON materialization

attack_steps: The operator configures and authorizes an online Mistral OCR operation for an eligible document.
The configured remote service, proxy, or intermediary accepts the authenticated request and slow-streams or returns an oversized or highly expanded response.
KCS reads and decompresses the complete JSON without a read or overall deadline or byte ceiling, then collects all pages, markdown, and images and decodes every base64 image.
Images are persisted before the caller's acceptance check, allowing the remote peer to hang the command or consume substantial memory, CPU, and disk.
assumptions: An operator-approved online OCR request is made.
The configured service, proxy, or intermediary is faulty, compromised, or hostile.
The response remains syntactically processable long enough to drive the unbounded sinks.
context: The remote adapter response is explicitly untrusted in the threat model even though the destination is operator-selected. The path affects availability and pre-acceptance storage during an approved outbound workflow; it does not bypass authorization or disclose data to a new origin.
in_scope: yes; remote response timing, size, decompression, cardinality, and persistence are explicit I6/I12 surfaces
exposure: outbound remote connection only; KCS has no public listener and the path begins after online-adapter approval
identity: KCS uses the victim OS identity and configured Mistral credential; the untrusted remote peer controls response timing and content but gains no additional local identity
cross_boundary: yes; authenticated remote response bytes cross the adapter boundary into local memory, CPU, and CAS disk writes
preconditions: plausible: an eligible approved OCR operation reaches a connected peer that can control the response; no local privilege or private-store write is required
attacker_control: yes; the connected remote peer controls response timing, wire/decompressed body size, pages, markdown, images, and base64 values
category: uncontrolled resource consumption from remote response (CWE-400, CWE-770)
mitigations: The supported CLI rechecks the local input cap before sending.
Connection establishment has a 30-second timeout.
Online approval, page-scoped requests, JSON shape checks, content-addressed deduplication, and atomic publication narrow the path.
auth_scope: internal-only; operator-approved authenticated adapter operation, not a public inbound endpoint
impact_surface: runtime memory, CPU, command availability, store-lock duration, and archive disk usage
target_reach: one online OCR command, its selected scope, and image CAS per malicious response
secrets_references: The configured Mistral API credential and document body are sent to the already approved origin; no unintended credential recipient was established.
counterevidence: The outbound request body is bounded by effective_max_input_bytes on the shipped CLI path.
Later acceptance checks can reject bad semantic output, but run only after response allocation and image persistence.
A well-behaved provider ordinarily constrains responses, but the threat model treats provider behavior as untrusted.
blindspots: No loopback slow-read or oversized-body measurement was retained; the exact resource constants remain unmeasured.
controls: online opt-in and current input-size check
rationale: A remote adapter response is a realistic in-scope attacker source once an ordinary approved OCR request occurs. The path is bounded to availability and disk effects, and the required matrix maps medium impact plus high likelihood to medium.

title: Default XDG config scope can ingest and embed `tools.toml` credentials
attack_steps: The operator deliberately selects the effective $HOME/.config/kcs directory as a KCS content scope.
The scanner's XDG exclusion and filename classifier fail to treat tools.toml as device configuration or a secret, although the preview lists the filename.
The operator explicitly enables online enrichment and the text-sniffing path normalizes and chunks tools.toml.
Gemini embedding serialization sends the file text, potentially including plain credentials for other providers, to the configured provider.
assumptions: The operator chooses the credential/configuration directory itself as the archive scope.
tools.toml contains plain credentials or adjacent sensitive configuration.
The operator sees the candidate name and still grants online enrichment.
context: The implementation has a real self-exclusion and secret-classification gap, and bytes can cross the network boundary. However, the saved evidence establishes only an operator-selected self-scope followed by explicit operator approval; it does not establish a lower-trust actor who can cause or control that choice.
in_scope: implemented scan and embedding components are in scope, but the evidenced attacker story is operator-only and fails final reportability policy
exposure: not public; locally selected config scope followed by an explicitly approved outbound embedding request
identity: the same trusted operator controls the scope, device configuration, provider selection, credential file, and online approval
cross_boundary: yes mechanically; local device credentials can reach an external provider, but the crossing is reached only through the operator's explicit scope and network choices
preconditions: operator-only and highly constraining: intentionally index the KCS credential directory, retain tools.toml, approve online enrichment, and configure a provider
attacker_control: no; no realistic lower-privileged actor controlling the source selection or approval was established
category: sensitive-data exposure caused by missing device-config exclusion and secret classification
mitigations: The preview visibly lists tools.toml.
Online enrichment requires explicit opt-in.
Offline mode, revocation, missing adapter configuration, or an explicit ignore rule prevents the sink.
A provider already receives its own credential as authentication; the clearest incremental impact is cross-provider disclosure.
impact_surface: device credential confidentiality and outbound embedding data
target_reach: one operator-selected config scope and its tools.toml contents
secrets_references: potential multiple-provider credentials and adjacent adapter configuration
counterevidence: KCS has no daemon or remote entrypoint that selects the scope.
No lower-trust contributor path to the private config file was shown.
The operator both chooses the unusual self-scope and authorizes the network operation.
blindspots: No loopback end-to-end capture was retained, though the static data flow is complete.
No deployment evidence shows automation selecting this scope without equivalent operator authority.
confidence: high (0.85) in the bug path; high in operator-only suppression
rationale: Hard suppression applies before the matrix: the only evidenced path requires the trusted operator to select the credential directory and explicitly approve online processing, with no realistic lower-privileged attacker. Intrinsic credential impact does not overcome an operator-only precondition.

affected_locations.label: Gemini POST and full JSON materialization

KCS sends a one-item query or at-most-32-item index batch to the configured remote service.
The service, proxy, or intermediary slow-streams or returns an oversized or highly compressed JSON response.

KCS fully reads, decompresses, and materializes the response before count, numeric-type, and dimension checks, allowing the remote peer to block the operation or consume substantial transient resources.
assumptions: An operator-approved Gemini query or indexing request is made.
The connected provider, proxy, or intermediary is faulty, compromised, or hostile.
context: The attack is limited to pre-validation availability. Invalid vectors are not persisted, query errors can fall back to text, and the fixed adopted model avoids model-resolution risk, but a connected peer still controls synchronous response time and allocation.
in_scope: yes; untrusted remote response timing and body expansion are explicit I6/I12 surfaces
exposure: outbound remote embedding request after adapter activation and authorization; no public inbound endpoint
identity: KCS uses the victim OS identity and configured Gemini credential; the remote peer controls only response behavior
cross_boundary: yes; untrusted remote response bytes cross into victim-process memory, CPU, and command latency before semantic validation

title: Opening an existing permissive `.kcs` exposes future private archive bytes

affected_locations.label: creation_control
affected_locations.detail: Existing .kcs returns through open before the new-store owner-only hardening call.

affected_locations.label: root_control
affected_locations.detail: Repository::open checks is_dir and logical store validity but no owner UID or permission mode.

affected_locations.label: owner_hardening
affected_locations.detail: The available Unix helper sets 0700 and documents the multi-user confidentiality boundary.

affected_locations.label: raw_source
affected_locations.detail: Snapshot reads direct-child bytes and sends them to ObjectStore.

affected_locations.label: raw_sink
affected_locations.detail: Raw CAS publication uses File::create/umask and relies on the parent store mode for confidentiality.

attack_steps: A lower-trust participant supplies, precreates, or influences a structurally valid existing .kcs store whose Unix ownership or permissions do not provide the expected owner-only boundary.
The victim adopts the scope and Repository::open accepts the store without rejecting or repairing its owner, type, or mode.
The victim later snapshots or indexes a private direct-child file while using an ordinary permissive umask.
KCS writes verbatim raw bytes as a group/world-readable CAS object beneath a traversable store, allowing a different local principal to read data that remained private at the source path.
assumptions: A multi-principal Unix host or shared filesystem enforces ordinary DAC semantics.
The victim adopts a valid existing store that is writable by KCS but readable or traversable by the lower-trust principal.
The victim later adds private content and the process umask does not independently force 0600 objects.
context: This is not same-user arbitrary mutation of a private live store. It uses the threat model's in-scope supplied/preseeded-store actor and crosses a distinct Unix principal boundary when KCS adds new private bytes after unsafe adoption.
in_scope: yes; pre-existing store adoption, owner-only archive confidentiality, and shared-state contributors are explicit I1/I3 surfaces
exposure: not public; local multi-user or shared-filesystem store reached through normal init/open and snapshot/index commands
identity: the victim KCS process writes with the victim OS identity; a lower-privileged local principal reads through unsafe store and object modes
cross_boundary: yes; victim-only source bytes become readable across an OS-principal filesystem boundary
preconditions: plausible but constrained: unsafe supplied or pre-existing store, victim adoption and later mutation, multi-principal access, and a non-0077 umask
attacker_control: plausible; the lower-trust archive contributor can control or preserve the supplied store's ownership/mode state without needing victim credentials
category: improper ownership and permission validation causing sensitive-data exposure (CWE-276, CWE-732)
mitigations: Fresh stores are explicitly hardened to 0700.
Repository open validates logical store structure.
A 0077 process umask can incidentally produce owner-only raw files.
The demonstrated path is Unix-specific and read-only trusted archives are a legitimate use case.
auth_scope: internal-only; lower-privileged local filesystem principal, not administrator or same-user unrestricted private-state access
impact_surface: archive confidentiality and integrity on multi-user filesystems
target_reach: all new raw objects written into one unsafely adopted store; the retained proof demonstrated one private file
secrets_references: Raw CAS objects contain verbatim document bytes and may include document secrets.
counterevidence: No second OS-account read was executed, though the observed 0600 source, 0755 store, and 0644 raw object establish the Unix DAC result.
A 0077 umask or a securely permissioned trusted store defeats the demonstrated confidentiality path.
Exposure of bytes already present before open is not attributed to KCS; the validated impact is new bytes written after adoption.
blindspots: Non-Unix ACL and ownership behavior was not assessed.
The exact supplied-store transfer mechanism and principal layout remain deployment-specific.
confidence: high (0.97) for the Unix mechanism; medium-high for deployment reachability
rationale: A supplied-store contributor and a different local OS principal are realistic in-scope actors, so privileged-only suppression does not apply. The disclosure can include private documents, but requires local setup and victim adoption; high impact plus medium likelihood maps to medium.

Offline mode and network revocation are not active.

Documentation treats .kcs as portable authoritative state, creating ambiguity for trusted moves but not authenticating an untrusted import.

impact_surface: network authorization, secret-release policy, and confidentiality of content in one adopted scope

Forged approval can release secret-bearing data, but adoption and a later configured online workflow constrain likelihood; high impact plus medium likelihood maps to medium.

title: Scan-time replacement can authorize an outside-scope file under a benign name

affected_locations.detail: Non-preview index asks the scanner to compute raw hashes for selected-root candidates.

affected_locations.label: root_control

affected_locations.label: hash_acceptance
